notes.text: NB: a mdynh is the large "capital" city of an administrative unit which can also be referred to by the same name/term, just as city-states in Antiquity were often called by the name of their capital city. In later periods a qryh is one of a number of large towns within such a unit, though in BA and earlier it can clearly be such a capital whereas mdynh refers to a province itself in such periods. By later times in Syriac it would seem that our word can also be used for any (larger?) unwalled settlement, i.e. "town" or "village", for which see U. Seidel, Altorientalische Forschungen 15(1988):143f., 152f. (but compare s.v. šṭḥ), or, as discussed below, for a "field". See also s.v. qry #3 n.f. The distinctive Syriac usage "field" is due to the similar semantic fields of the Greek underlying the early translations; compare the loanword Ɂgwrs. The various plurals in Syriac seem to be used differently by different authors; see, e.g., IshNum 114:29: ܐܓܘܪ̈ܣܐܼ ܩܘܪ̈ܝܣ܂ ܟܦܪ̈ܘܢܐܼ ܩܘܪ̈ܝܐ ܕܩܕܩ̈ܬܐ

notes.text: Greek κύβος. The definition "hard stone, flint" given in SL from LS2 is yet another example of the plethora of falsely derived glosses in Brockelmann's praise-laden work. The main text of the Syro-hexapla is a translation of the Septuagint, it is not a translation of the Masoretic Text! Neither the Greek etymon of this loanword nor the meaning of the form it translates from the Septuagint supports such a gloss. Note, however, that even some of the most modern dictionaries of the Septuagint are not totally immune to the 19th century habit of adding a gloss to conform somewhat to the biblical text: see e.g. for the latter word GLS s.v. ψῆφος,-ου: "pebble, gravel Lam 3,16; grain (of sand) Sir 18,10; sharp stone (used as a knife) Ex 4,25; pebble used in voting, vote 4 Mc 15,26; account Eccl 7,25."

text.text: wlʕnw dwšrʾ wmnwtw wqyšh kl mn dy yzbn kprʾ dnh

citations.translation: may Dushara, Manawa, and alQays curse whoever sells this tomb

notes.text: Possibly to be read as קלוטין, i.e., a pl. tant.. As shown by Amit Gvaryahu in Lesh 79 (2018):247ff., the Talmudic Hebrew equivalent of this expression refers to a special dispensation for excessive interest involved in overseas mercantile transactions, a usage probably influenced by (hardly a loanword!) the similar-sounding Latin term collocatum . One of these Semitic usages is obviously a play on the other, but which way the relationship goes is not clear.

notes.text: For the Palestinian usage "to behead" compare s.v. qdl. Note the distinction between the G and D stems as taken up by BarBahlul extensively. The two cited passages from GT AA Exod12 demonstrate an often overlooked grammatical pattern in PTA, i.e. that the derived stem infinitive when alone usually is of the Palestinian type with initial mem and final -ā but with pronominal suffixes follows the JLA pattern without mem and with final -ā replaced by -ūṯ_. This patterning was overlooked by DJPA by treating all these forms as nouns ending in -ū.

notes.text: Syriac lexicographers, both native and modern, combined two etymologically separate roots 1) to tie into knots (=Akkadian kaṣāru, Heb. קשׁר) and 2) to burn incense (= Akk.qatāru, Heb. קטר ), that have here been disambiguated. All meanings involving the idea of "condensation" belong here, but the common semantic development in Syriac into "force" in the participial form qṭyr and related words is not easily assigned to one meaning or the other, hence, perhaps, the lexicographical confusion.

notes.text: Many of the plethora of meanings ascribed to this verb in DJBA belong rather to the simple sense "to be present", while the special meaning is in fact conveyed by the preposition or the nominal relations. The pael meaning "to swear", "make a covenant" may be understood as separate denominatives from qyām "covenant". Students of Hebrew should note the difference between that language and Aramaic here: In BH קום is "to arise, stand up" while "to stand, stop" is עמד. In Aramaic קום is used for both of these senses.
